title: When Gaussian kernel spaces are invariant under stochastic dynamics: transition rigidity, a Gaussian-component noise boundary and a discontinuous diffusion limit
shortTitle: The factor is 4, not 2: when Gaussian kernel spaces survive random dynamics
oneLine: A Gaussian kernel space is invariant under an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process exactly when AP + PAᵀ ⪯ 4BBᵀ, twice the range of the earlier sufficient condition, and among Gaussian or fixed-noise transitions only affine maps can preserve it at all.
abstract: Kernel methods such as kernel EDMD learn how a random system evolves by working inside the reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) of a Gaussian kernel, and their error analysis often assumes the dynamics keep that space invariant. Philipp et al. (2025, PAMM) proved invariance for linear stochastic differential equations (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes) when AP + PAᵀ ⪯ 2BBᵀ and left open whether this is necessary. This candidate shows that the exact condition is AP + PAᵀ ⪯ 4BBᵀ; a stable controllable shear separates the two. More generally, a Markov transition with Gaussian conditional laws N(F(x), Q(x)) that maps one global Gaussian RKHS boundedly into another must have constant Q, affine F and MRMᵀ ⪯ P + 4Q; a transition of the form map plus fixed noise, for noise whose characteristic function has a Gaussian lower bound (every infinitely divisible law, pure jumps included), must have an affine map, so Euler steps of nonlinear SDEs never preserve the space. For affine maps with infinitely divisible noise only the Gaussian covariance component counts, and a compound-Poisson approximation of a stable linear diffusion converges at sharp order ε² in prediction while every approximant sends one fixed Gaussian observable out of the space. Consequences include an exact bandwidth rule (twice the earlier range) and the invariance hypothesis of an existing kEDMD error bound for multivariate OU processes. The fixed affine criterion specialises classical Gaussian-Fock theory, and the separating witness with a proposed derivation was posted first, explicitly unproven, in a GitHub issue. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Gaussian transition rigidity (Theorem 5, proof): a transition with Gaussian conditional laws N(F(x), Q(x)), arbitrary Borel fields, maps one global Gaussian RKHS boundedly into another only if Q is constant, F is affine with full-column-rank matrix M, and MRMᵀ ⪯ P + 4Q.

Additive-noise rigidity (Theorem 9, proof): with fixed noise whose characteristic function has a Gaussian lower bound (every infinitely divisible law, pure jumps included) the drift must be affine; for affine maps only the Gaussian covariance component enters the boundary (Theorems 8, 11).

Ornstein–Uhlenbeck answer (Theorem 6, proof): all-time invariance holds exactly when AP + PAᵀ ⪯ 4BBᵀ; the shear A = [[−1, 5], [0, −1]], B = P = I satisfies it but not the factor-2 condition of Philipp et al. (2025). This specialises classical Gaussian-Fock theory; the witness was proposed first in a GitHub issue.

Discontinuous diffusion limit (Theorem 12, Proposition 13, proof and quadrature): compound-Poisson approximants converge at sharp order ε² from the RKHS to bounded continuous functions, yet at t = 1/10 each sends exp(−8|x|²/5) outside the space.

Bandwidth rule (Proposition 17, Corollary 18): isotropic widths σ² ≤ 4/λmax are admissible, twice the earlier range (shear: 4/3, not 2/3), so a published kEDMD error bound applies to multivariate OU processes.

narration:
This is a short audio briefing on a new Evidence Press research candidate: when Gaussian kernel spaces are invariant under stochastic dynamics.

Some machine-learning methods learn how a random system evolves by working inside a space of smooth test functions, built from a Gaussian kernel. Their error guarantees often assume that the dynamics keep this space invariant: average any function in the space over one step of the random motion, and you should land back inside the space.

In 2025, Philipp and colleagues proved that this holds for linear stochastic systems, the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck processes, under a matrix condition with a factor of two, and they asked whether that condition is also necessary. This paper answers no. The exact condition has a factor of four instead. The reason is simple: the norm of the space compares two independent copies of the noise, and their difference has twice the variance. A stable shear system shows the gap. For it, the largest admissible kernel width doubles, from two thirds to four thirds.

The paper then goes further. Among transitions whose random steps are Gaussian, and among transitions made of a fixed map plus independent noise of a broad kind, including jump noise, only affine maps can keep a Gaussian kernel space invariant. So Euler steps of nonlinear equations never do. For linear systems driven by jump noise, only the Gaussian part of the noise matters. And a jump approximation of a Brownian system can converge very fast in prediction while every approximation still pushes one fixed function out of the space.

Some limits. The factor-four criterion itself is a translation of classical results on Gaussian operators in Fock space, by Neretin and others, and the shear example and a proposed derivation were posted first, explicitly unproven, in a public GitHub issue on 28 October 2026. The statements concern the global norm of the space, not pointwise prediction or learning from finite data, and state-dependent non-Gaussian transitions remain open.

The proofs are written out in full, and the scripts check the constants exactly where possible. Review was internal and AI-assisted. This remains an unrefereed candidate.

This briefing uses a synthetic voice, and it is not additional scientific evidence.

decisionObject.description: Which stochastic transitions keep a global Gaussian RKHS invariant: exactly affine Gaussian or affine infinitely divisible transitions with MRMᵀ ⪯ P + 4Q (Gaussian part only); for OU processes AP + PAᵀ ⪯ 4BBᵀ.
